usedHookFrames: Your brain is not tired from the work, it is tired from holding every loose promise at once.
The scrap in your pocket is not small until it has passed through a place you trust.
The project is not stuck in your calendar, it is stuck in the fog between a wish and a first move.
Before you can clear your head, you need a flat surface, a quiet hour, and a place for every loose promise.
The note you trust to memory during a busy shift is already halfway to being lost.
The pile on your counter is not work yet, it is a row of small decisions waiting to be named.
The same sticky note cannot hold a court date, a phone call, and a hope for later.
The list you trusted on Monday can start lying to you quietly by Friday.
Your to-do list is not a to-do list. It is a menu, and half the items are not available from where you are sitting right now.
Your project list has a line that has been there for weeks, and staring at it has never once moved it forward.
Every item you are mentally rehearsing right now is costing you something, and none of it is moving.
Your list is full of things you care about and empty of things you can do.
You cannot track a commitment that has no close condition, and most of yours do not have one.
usedCounterFrames: Most people assume overload comes from having too much to do. Allen’s sharper claim is that vague, unparked commitments create the strain: the court call, school form, sink leak, and invoice all keep tugging until each has a visible place you trust.

Most people try to feel in control by ranking what is already shouting. Allen starts earlier: capture first, then decide what each item means, where it belongs, and when you will see it again. Priority works only after the workflow stops leaking.

Most people try to rescue a stalled project by tightening the plan too early. Allen's move is stranger and more useful: clarify why it matters, picture success, let ideas spill loosely, then organize only enough to name the next physical action.

Setting up trays, folders, and a work surface can look like avoidance when the pile is already urgent. In GTD, it is the first practical move, because a system cannot earn trust if capture and clarification are awkward from the start.

Most people start by sorting, answering, or doing the loudest item. Allen's odd discipline is to collect first without judging, because an uncaptured promise keeps using your attention even if you have not decided what it means.
Getting an inbox to empty does not mean finishing everything in it. It means refusing to touch the same item twice without deciding what it is, what action it needs, and where its reminder will live.

A single master list feels responsible because everything is in one place. In practice, it makes every item compete by volume, so a hard deadline, a waiting reply, and a someday idea all nag you in the same voice.

Reviewing feels like maintenance you do after the real work, but in GTD it is what makes the work possible. A stale list is just another inbox in disguise, so the weekly review is where you decide what is current, what is waiting, and what can safely stay undone.

Most people treat choosing the next action as a priority problem: rank everything by importance, do the top item. But importance is not the binding constraint. Context, time, and energy determine what is even eligible, and a high-priority task you cannot do from here costs you nothing to ignore until you can.

Most people assume a stalled project needs more time or motivation. It needs neither: it needs two minutes to write one sentence about what done looks like and one sentence about the next physical action. The project was never stuck, the definition was.

Most people assume the problem is forgetting: write it down so you don't lose it. The actual problem is remembering: your mind keeps recirculating unfinished items not because it is disorganized, but because it is doing exactly what you trained it to do. Capture doesn't save your memory from failure. It releases your mind from a job it was never supposed to hold.

Most people assume a stalled project means low motivation or too little time. It usually means the list item is an outcome disguised as a task, and no amount of caring moves an outcome. The moment you name the physical action, urgency becomes irrelevant: you either do it or you choose not to, and both are decisions you can actually make.

Most people assume the problem is not knowing what to do next. It is not. The problem is that 'done' was never defined, so the system has nothing to track toward and the mind keeps the loop open regardless of how much action happens.
usedTryThisNowFrames: Take out your phone and open your notes app. Write down the first three things that are nagging at you right now, then save it. Notice how it feels to get them out of your head.
In the next minute, pick one task from your to-do list. Write down the next physical action you can take to move it forward. Place it in a visible spot to remind you.
Look at the first stalled project on your list. In 60 seconds, write down one clear next physical action you can take to move it forward. Keep it simple and specific.
Look at your calendar for the next hour. Identify one commitment you can write down in a trusted place. Do it now and notice how it feels to capture that thought.
Take a minute to gather any loose commitments from your mind right now. Write down three of them in a visible spot, like a sticky note or a digital note app.
Open your email and pick the last unread message. Decide if it's actionable, what the next step is, and where you'll put a reminder for it. Do this in under 90 seconds.
Look at your to-do list or calendar. Pick one item that feels vague or overwhelming. Choose a specific bucket for it, like 'next actions' or 'projects', and move it there now.
Take a moment to look at your to-do list or reminders. Identify one task that feels incomplete or outdated, and either complete it now or remove it from your list. Notice how that feels.
Open your inbox right now. What calls first: newest, scariest, or most important? Pick the next action by your available time and energy instead. Notice what you chose differently.

Take a project you've been avoiding. Spend two minutes: write what done looks like, list every moving piece, circle one action. Notice whether the project unsticks or you discover why you've really been stuck.
Open the email or tab you keep returning to. Type what's unresolved into your notes. Three words is enough, then close it.
Open the last task you postponed. What exact physical move would begin it? Say that answer out loud. Notice how much clearer the choice just got.
Find the task you've been stuck on. Say what done is. One sentence. Then pick your first move. Notice what changed.
